item.title: Elderly couple devastated after Suva home broken into three times within four days
item.description: The couple, who have asked not to be named, say they were overseas when they started receiving information that people had entered their home and stolen a number of items. They say the first break-in happened last weekend before the intruders returned twice over the following days.
item.content:encoded:
The couple, who have asked not to be named, say they were overseas when they started receiving information that people had entered their home and stolen a number of items.

They say the first break-in happened last weekend before the intruders returned twice over the following days.

The couple say the intruders gained access from the Terry Walk side of the property and climbed two storeys along the exterior of the building to reach the home.

They say structural pipes and louvres were damaged in the process, while a door was also damaged.

The residents say boxes of ghee, liquor and other kitchen and household items were stolen.

They say the intruders also attempted to take heavy items, including LPG gas cylinders and a microwave, which they say were wrapped in bedsheets and left behind.

The residents believe the items may have been left there to be collected later.

They say their caretaker reinforced the entry points and moved items following the incidents.

One of the residents says this is the first time they have experienced something like this at the property in about 70 years.

Insert: Resident on robbery 20 September, 26

He says returning to see the condition of their home has been extremely difficult, particularly for his wife, who has been badly affected by what happened.

The family has also raised concerns for relatives who are expected to return to the property this Sunday, saying they fear for their safety.

The residents say the frequency of the break-ins has left them concerned that future incidents could result in confrontations, serious injuries or loss of life if the security situation is not addressed.

They have also raised concerns about the lack of lighting along Terry Walk behind their building.

They say they had repeatedly contacted the Suva City Council asking for a streetlight behind the property to be fixed and for an overgrown guava tree close to the building to be cut.

They believe the tree may have been used to gain access to the upper level of the building.

The resident says the area becomes very dark at night and believes better lighting could improve security for people living and working in the area.

The residents have also raised concerns about alleged drug-related activity along Terry Walk, particularly near the EFL substation, and are calling for greater Police presence in the area.

They are also calling for increased CCTV coverage in the Suva CBD, saying this could assist authorities in identifying and tracking people involved in criminal activity.

The residents say three break-ins at the same property within four days have heightened their concerns about security and they want immediate and visible action to improve safety in the area.

The couple say Police visited the property earlier today to inspect the scene and were expected to return for further investigations.

They are calling for stronger security measures and greater attention to safety concerns in the area.

item.title: WOWS Kids Fiji co-founders turn loss into mission to help children
item.description: More than 18 years after losing their eldest daughter Tae Kami to cancer, Taholo and Sina Kami, co-founders of WOWS Kids Fiji, say her voice, faith and determination continue to guide their work, as they hope the mission she inspired will continue long after they are gone. Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan , the couple reflected on their eldest daughter Tae’s cancer journey,
item.content:encoded:
More than 18 years after losing their eldest daughter Tae Kami to cancer, Taholo and Sina Kami, co-founders of WOWS Kids Fiji, say her voice, faith and determination continue to guide their work, as they hope the mission she inspired will continue long after they are gone.

Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan , the couple reflected on their eldest daughter Tae’s cancer journey, from the first signs to her diagnosis, treatment and the legacy she left behind.

Tae's father, Taholo says his wife was the first to notice that Tae was having repeated nosebleeds and kept telling him that she believed something was wrong.

Insert: Taholo on his daughter's early stage of cancer 19th Sept

Doctors initially suspected the tumour could be cancer because it kept growing back, with specialists in New Zealand later confirming the diagnosis after further tests.

Sina says Tae herself asked whether it was cancer, and despite the diagnosis, told her mother she was not going to give up.

Taholo says the diagnosis brought some answers but also fear and uncertainty, as the family learned Tae would need major surgery with significant costs.

Taholo says he and Sina were both working for the church on church salaries at the time, and this was when the reality of what the family was facing began to hit home.

Following Tae’s death, the couple turned their grief into a mission to help other children with cancer and continue the message their daughter had left behind.

Sina says after returning following Tae’s burial, she attended a Fiji Cancer Society meeting and realised there was no specific fund dedicated to children with cancer.

She says while funds were available, the money raised was being used to support both adults and children.

Sina says she and Taholo began discussing what they could do in Tae’s memory when they returned for her first anniversary.

She says they went through Tae’s writings and belongings and realised they could use her message to start what became the Walk On, Walk Strong Fiji initiative.

The couple also held a WOWS Tonga event for Tae’s first anniversary.

Sina says they agreed to use Tae’s song and message to raise funds, with the money initially going to the Fiji Cancer Society to help children with cancer.

She says WOWS was not registered as an organisation at the time, but they were later asked to register it, leading to the establishment of WOWS Kids Fiji.

Sina says WOWS Kids Fiji now supports children with cancer, while the Fiji Cancer Society looks after adults.

She says establishing the organisation was not easy, particularly as they faced questions about why they were doing the work and whether they were doing it for their own benefit.

She says they remained focused on Tae’s dream, while support from people in Fiji helped them continue their work.

item.title: El Niño dry spell puts Lautoka farmers and livestock under pressure
item.description: The effects of the El Niño dry spell are becoming increasingly visible across Fiji’s Western Division, with Lautoka resident Navneet Ram raising concerns over worsening dry conditions and their impact on farmers and livestock. Ram says areas including Teidamu, Drasa and Raviravi are experiencing severe dryness and reduced rainfall, putting additional pressure on agricultural communities.
item.content:encoded:
The effects of the El Niño dry spell are becoming increasingly visible across Fiji’s Western Division, with Lautoka resident Navneet Ram raising concerns over worsening dry conditions and their impact on farmers and livestock.

Ram says areas including Teidamu, Drasa and Raviravi are experiencing severe dryness and reduced rainfall, putting additional pressure on agricultural communities.

He says the prolonged dry spell is affecting not only sugarcane farms but also the availability of fresh produce, with a noticeable decrease in the supply of vegetables.

Ram says the lack of sufficient rainfall is placing farmers under increasing pressure as they struggle to maintain crops and livestock in the dry conditions.

He says the conditions have also increased agricultural risks, including the threat of sugarcane farm fires in some areas.

Ram says for farmers, the effects of a failed or prolonged dry season go beyond the environment, as reduced agricultural production can directly affect household food supplies and income.

He says the continued dry conditions are a growing concern for rural communities across the Western Division as the impact of El Niño becomes more evident.

item.title: 44 PSV drivers trained to provide First Aid and CPR during road emergencies
item.description: 44 Public Service Vehicle (PSV) drivers across Fiji are now better equipped to respond to emergencies on the country’s roads after successfully completing a free two-day First Aid and CPR training programme delivered by the Fiji Red Cross Society. The programme equipped drivers with essential knowledge and practical skills to respond to medical emergencies and road accidents.
item.content:encoded:
44 Public Service Vehicle (PSV) drivers across Fiji are now better equipped to respond to emergencies on the country’s roads after successfully completing a free two-day First Aid and CPR training programme delivered by the Fiji Red Cross Society.

The programme equipped drivers with essential knowledge and practical skills to respond to medical emergencies and road accidents.

As PSV drivers spend much of their time on the road, they can often be among the first people to arrive at the scene of a road accident.

The training aims to give drivers the confidence and skills to provide immediate assistance, reduce panic and help stabilise casualties while waiting for professional emergency medical services to arrive.

One of the participants, Penina Temo, says she had always wanted to learn First Aid and CPR but had never had the opportunity.

She says she was on her way to work with her husband when he told her about the free training being offered by the Red Cross.

Reflecting on the two-day training, Temo says the knowledge and skills she gained would be valuable both on the road and at home.

She says the training has helped her better understand how to respond correctly and use the necessary skills to prevent further chaos at an accident scene before professional help arrives.

The training was held simultaneously in Suva and Lautoka as part of activities marking World First Aid Day, with 19 PSV drivers participating in Suva and 25 in Lautoka.

The Fiji Red Cross Society covered the full cost of the programme, including training materials, facilitation and certification, allowing the drivers to participate at no cost.

First Aid and CPR training of this nature normally comes at a cost, and many PSV drivers had never previously had the opportunity to access such training.

Participants completed theoretical and practical sessions covering accident scene management, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), choking and the control of severe bleeding.

Those who successfully completed the training were awarded certificates.

item.title: Labour shortage pushes Korovuto cane farmers towards mechanical harvesting
item.description: The Korovuto Cane Farmers Co-operative Limited has received the harvester, valued at $383,000, to serve its members and other farmers in the Rarawai Mill area. Co-operative member Amrit Singh says finding workers has become increasingly difficult, while harvesting costs continue to put pressure on farmers.
item.content:encoded:
The Korovuto Cane Farmers Co-operative Limited has received the harvester, valued at $383,000, to serve its members and other farmers in the Rarawai Mill area.

Co-operative member Amrit Singh says finding workers has become increasingly difficult, while harvesting costs continue to put pressure on farmers.

The Government contributed $150,000 towards the harvester through the Integrated Human Resource Development Programme.

Sugar Cane Growers Council CEO Bimal Dutt says labour shortages have become a serious issue for the sugar industry, making mechanisation increasingly important.

The new harvester has also created three jobs, including a full-time machine operator and two assistants.

The Korovuto Cane Farmers Co-operative was registered in November 2024 with 11 members and has since grown to 22 members .

Each member has contributed $1,500 in shares to the co-operative.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce and Business Development Manoa Kamikamica says the project is a joint investment between the Government and farmers rather than simply a handout.

The co-operative now plans to acquire a cane truck and eventually other farming machinery, including a tractor.
